attempts.raw_response: If you or someone in your household relies on specialized medical equipment, ensure you have backup power sources, such as generators or extra batteries, and keep a list of emergency contacts for equipment repairs. Maintain a two-week supply of medications and any necessary medical supplies, and talk to your doctor about obtaining early refills if possible. Establish a communication plan with family, neighbors, or caregivers who can check in regularly. Identify alternative care options, such as home health aides or telehealth services, and discuss contingency plans with your support network. Finally, keep important documents, like medical records and care instructions, easily accessible in a waterproof container.

pair.human_continuation: Consider other ways to get to work or, if you can, work at home. Ask your employer about how business will continue during a pandemic. The U.S. Department of Health & Human Services offers a Business Pandemic Influenza Planning Checklist; or you can Develop a Risk Management Plan that accounts for the possibility of a flu pandemic. Find out if you can work from home, or if your employer will consider virtualizing the workforce. Plan for the possible reduction or loss of income if you are unable to work or your place of employment is closed. Check with your employer or union about leave policies. Reduce exposure at work by using virtual workforce technologies. Use email, web conferencing and Pixetell enhanced documents to maintain effective business interactions without shaking so many hands.
pair.prefix: Make plans for how to care for people with special needs in case the services they rely on are not available. Transportation networks are disrupted: Think about how you can rely less on public transportation during a pandemic as this typically is a time when you have considerable contact with potentially contaminated surfaces and people and thus risk infection. For example, store food and other essential supplies to reduce shopping trips.
